groups.title: Results Ordered: Yes, then No, then not finished; each by the change in risks found. Not a ranking.

head: The setup tested: the model and its setting. Tap or point at a name for its details.

Yes: the change in risks found is above the threshold and right safety falls by no more than 5 pp. No: either fails. Shown once every run is complete; before that, the model's state (running, queued, waiting and why, not tested and the rule).
Risks found after the series minus before, in percentage points (pp): points of the share, not a relative percent.
Took the risk when it paid, as a share of the positions where it did: before = the mean of its 3 empty runs (no lessons), after = after the series of lessons.
Right safety (played safe when safe was right) after minus before, in percentage points. A fall of more than 5 pp makes the result No.
What the change must beat: the larger of the model's own spread over its 3 empty runs (max − min of risks found) and 5 pp.
Improved: Yes

blocks.p: No model of this kind in the plan.

49 chat models under the pre-registered rule. Threshold = what the change must beat: the spread (max − min) of the model's own risks found over its 3 empty runs (in each row's details), at least 5 points; right safety may fall by at most 5 points. Rows marked "planned, not a result" are not run yet and show no numbers; a decision setup has one row per arm (notes, worst mistakes).

blocks.h: Result: Yes or No once every run is complete; the change, right safety change and threshold are in points (pp). *

blocks.p: Threshold: the larger of the model's own spread over its three empty runs (max − min) and 5 points; right safety may fall by at most 5 points.

blocks.h: Class: by the maker's total parameters, or by list price when the size is undisclosed *

blocks.p: Size by total parameters, as disclosed by the maker (for MoE models the label also shows active parameters): Tiny under 6B · Small 6B–15B · Medium over 15B up to 40B · Large over 40B. How a model is judged. It answers the 200-position risk test 3 times with no memory (before = the mean of those empty runs), then plays 5 series of 10 games against GNUbg weak, writing its own lessons after each game, and takes the test again after game 10 of each series (after = the mean of the 5). Improved? is Yes when risks found rises by more than the improvement threshold (the spread, max − min, of its own 3 empty runs, at least 5 points) and right safety falls by no more than 5 points. This is an operational threshold, not a statistical test. Yes or No only once every run is complete.
The results as each model's runs come in, and every lesson. Data: improve.json.

Added 12 Nov, after the plan was published: the Tiny and Small chat models tested on Logic & Math, each at its highest reasoning setting, under the same rule, lesson prompt, test and schedule. Listed here once the setup's settings are in the league database; Gemma 4 12B, Erk-14B and Qwen3-14B follow when theirs are. (Ümit's decision of 12 Nov 2026.)

Added 20 Nov: the small models of 2B or less on our own GPU (LFM3-1.7B also with thinking off, Qwen3.5-2B, Raon-1 nano, SmolLM2-1.7B, SmolLM2-360M), under the same rule, lesson prompt, test and schedule, each with the settings of its league setup. For these and LFM3-1.7B, MiniCPM5-2B and Gemma 4 E2B, the first empty test is a validity check: a model with more than 10% invalid answers there (more than 20 of 200) stops and plays no series. Then SmolLM3-3B with thinking on, with the card's sampling (temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95), its first empty test a validity check as above; with thinking off it runs the first empty test only, as a format check, and plays no series. On our own GPU, a model whose next lesson call or next game's lessons would not fit its context stops there with that reason; lessons are never shortened to fit. (Ümit's decisions of 20 Nov 2026.)

Added 21 Nov: Inkling 2 Mini with thinking on (effort 0.9), under the same rule, lesson prompt, test and schedule, on the server it shares with Logic & Math and other benchmarks (its owner's pinned load; this run neither starts nor stops it), sampled greedily as on Logic & Math (temperature 0), its first empty test a validity check as above. Its letter is read from its own answer after its reasoning: its server cannot continue a prefilled answer after a reasoning block. While that server is away, the model pauses. At effort 0.9, 110 of the first 148 answers used all 32,768 output tokens without naming an option; that run stopped and played no series. It was then rerun at effort 0.5, otherwise unchanged. That rerun also stopped at the validity check: 40 of 200 answers (20%) used all 32,768 output tokens without naming an option, above the 10% invalid-answer limit; it played no series. (Ümit's decision of 21 Nov 2026.)

Inkling 2 Mini retry order, decided before either retry's first call. A capped answer counts as a trailing loop when a pattern of at most 64 whitespace tokens reproduces at least 80% of its final 512 whitespace tokens. Of the capped answers, effort 0.9 had 31 loops and 79 still reasoning normally; effort 0.5 had 25 loops and 15 still reasoning normally. Combined, 56 of 150 were loops and 94 were still reasoning normally, so the lower-effort retry comes first. First try: effort 0.2, temperature 0 and the same 32,768-token limit. Its first empty run is the 200-position validity check; at most 20 invalid answers passes, then this setup plays the full schedule. If it fails, second try: effort 0.5 with the model card's complete sampling configuration (do_sample true, temperature 1.0, eos token 200006 and pad token 199999; the token ids are properties of the loaded server, and the request changes temperature from 0 to 1.0). The card specifies no top_p, top_k or min_p. This is a different setup from the Logic & Math row, which uses effort 0.9 and temperature 0. Sampling at temperature 1.0 can widen this setup's own three-empty-run spread and therefore raise its improvement threshold. Its first empty run uses the same validity check; if it passes, it plays the full schedule. If both retries fail, Inkling stops and is recorded as unable to take the test; there is no third setting. Exploratory 10-position probe, not a result: effort 0.9 with the card's temperature 1.0 returned 9 valid answers and had 1 answer reach the 32,768-token limit; mean output was about 19,500 tokens, median about 16,000 and the slowest request took 814 seconds. The probe was effort 0.9, not the second retry's effort 0.5. On 24 Nov, after Logic & Math's shared server was gone, Learning loaded one compatible copy on its reserved GPU 2 from the same pinned revision, image and server arguments. Logic disabled its pending GPU 1 copy; the GPU 3 small-model lane was not interrupted. The live load is shared with Logic, Compactor, Jack and Toolbench, which do not stop or restart it. Same-day Learning decision: Inkling keeps this evidence and first-retry priority. LFM2.5-24B-A2B thinking off runs on our GPU immediately after Qwen3.5-2B, with the 200-position validity check (at most 20 invalid passes) and the existing context-fit stop rule; lessons are never shortened. Four reasoning-high successors were planned at this decision: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol through the ChatGPT subscription with no explicit output-cap override; Gemini 4 Neon through Antigravity, thinking high with no explicit output-cap override; Claude Fable 5.2 through a separate Claude subscription, adaptive thinking at effort high with a 32,768-token output limit. Estimated full schedules: Astra / Sol about 2,700 requests and $180–$200 / $45–$50 API-list-price equivalent; Neon about 2,900 and $405–$410; Fable about 2,900 and $440–$445. These scale predecessor usage at current standard API input/output prices per million tokens: Astra $8/$40, Sol $2/$10, Neon $3/$15, Fable $8/$40; they are not quota guarantees. The later 24 Nov amendment records their approved starts. (Ümit's decision of 23 Nov 2026.)

Subscription successors moved from planned rows into the Learning roster: Gemini 4 Neon through Antigravity at thinking high; GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol through the ChatGPT/Codex route at reasoning high; Claude Fable 5.2 through the separate Claude subscription at adaptive-thinking effort high with a 32,768-token output limit. They use the same 50-game, 50-lesson and eight-test schedule. Subscription use is prioritized ahead of a new paid API route. Claude Opus 5.5 is not rerun because its existing Learning run is complete. (Ümit's subscription Learning decision of 24 Nov 2026.)

It runs after Gemini 4 Neon without interrupting Neon, under the same 50-game, 50-lesson and eight-test schedule. Its existing Antigravity smoke reply identifies itself as gemini-4-carbon. blocks.h: Series 1: 10 games, 2 won; 10 lesson calls, 0 cut, 0 empty; 0 restarts; game decisions 220, invalid 0

blocks.p: Game 1: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Hit when you can; you missed hitting chances three times (turns 9, 21, 39). Don't be too passive. - In the midgame, advance your most advanced outfield checkers rather than making home points (turn 17: 23/17 17/13 was far superior to clogging home). - When bearing off, always advance your most advanced checkers first instead of working on lower points — this was a recurring endgame error (turns 43, 45, 47, 49, 51).

blocks.p: Game 2: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When you have advanced checkers and the opponent is weak, push them forward aggressively instead of building slots in your home board; you missed this risk five times in the opening. - Hitting a blotto in your own territory is rarely the right move when an alternative exists to advance a back checker; look for the aggressive option first. - Repeated "missed risk" calls on consecutive turns mean your overall plan is too passive—reassess whether your strategy should be attacking rather than just responding. - In the endgame you played well, so the problem is specifically a mid-game aggression deficit, not a general weakness.

blocks.p: Game 3: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don't ignore your back checker. On four separate turns I left the 24-point stationary while working my home board. Advance it consistently. - When you have a reasonable prime, prefer advancing your outermost checkers toward bearing off over strengthening the prime further. - Actively look for hits. This game was full of "missed risk" — I was too passive and left winning touches on the table. - When bearing off, bear off from your lowest points rather than moving checkers up to higher points. - Your overall risk calibration is too cautious. Trust the hits and the advances; only play safe when the equity clearly demands it.

blocks.p: Game 4: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don't hit just because you can; hitting on easily-escaped points is needless risk. - Always advance your most advanced back checker before making home board points. - Bear off when possible; don't waste dice making unneeded points. - Advancing beats making points in most middlegame and bearing-off situations. - Before any hit, verify it creates a real tactical edge rather than just a blunder.

blocks.p: Game 5: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - In running games, bring down back checkers rather than making slots or primes with front checkers; this was my most repeated error. - When a hit is available, don't be overly passive—if the opponent's position is weak, hitting often wins even in a running game. - Conversely, don't hit blindly just because a blot is exposed; sometimes the prime is the better play. - In a running game, a prime built from front checkers is worth less than advancing your back checker toward home. - Always ask "does this move advance my back checker?" before committing to board structure.

blocks.p: Game 6: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Always look for a hit before playing safe. I missed clear hits on turns 10, 26, and 28; a hit sending a checker to the bar is usually the strongest move. - On doubles I tend to advance all four moves aggressively. Prioritize safe moves and building position over pushing checkers forward when the position is already solid. - Before advancing a checker, verify the opponent can't hit it at good value. I made needless risks on turns 6 and 32 where the advancement created a cheap hit. - When I hold a clear advantage (opponent checkers outside or on bar), convert by hitting rather than cautiously advancing my own checkers.

blocks.p: Game 7: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Prioritize bringing your outermost checkers into your prime over making inner-board moves, even when a hit is available. - When you have a backchecker on the 24-point, bring it home to join your prime (24/21) rather than making small advances or hits elsewhere. - In the endgame, advance your outermost checkers together rather than making small moves with checkers already in your inner board. - Don't over-hit in the midgame; prefer advancing your structure and building your prime when the opportunity is clear.

blocks.p: Game 8: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Always prioritize advancing your back checker; leaving a lone checker on 24 while working the home board cost the most equity in this game. - When re-entering from the bar with another back checker on 24, bring the new checker to 23 to stack rather than returning it to 24. - Do not over-invest in making or improving home-board points while a back checker remains stranded in the opponent's home board. - If you must choose between a safe home-board move and advancing a back checker, the back checker almost always wins.

blocks.p: Game 9: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - I'm too passive in the midgame: I repeatedly miss risk by defaulting to safe home-board moves instead of advancing mid checkers. - Don't waste moves on front checkers (22, 17) while mid checkers are still behind—develop the mid first. - When bearing off is available and you're ahead, bear off instead of chasing back checkers. - "Needless risk" calls reveal I'm hitting without strong follow-up—only hit when the position supports it. - With doubles, use them to advance the most important checkers (e.g., building a prime) rather than small safe steps.

blocks.p: Game 10: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When a hit is available and the position is favorable, take it — I missed four hits this game by playing safe. - Before making a hit, confirm it's the strongest one; I twice chose the wrong target. - Consolidate checkers in your home board to build a prime rather than leaving them scattered. - Move back checkers forward when the board allows; don't leave them stranded. - Don't make unnecessary blots when a safe play exists; verify you're not creating a blot for no gain.

blocks.h: Series 2: 10 games, 4 won; 10 lesson calls, 0 cut, 0 empty; 0 restarts; game decisions 239, invalid 0

blocks.p: Game 1: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - In the opening, prioritize building your prime and inner board over small advances. - When you have a safe position and can hit a blot, take the hit — you missed hitting opportunities repeatedly. - In the bearing-off phase, always bring down the furthest checkers first. - Don't be overcautious: "missed risk" appeared four times, showing you default to safety when aggression is warranted. - When bearing off, avoid creating new blots on checkers that aren't yet ready to bear off.

blocks.p: Game 2: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - I'm too passive: "missed risk" is my dominant error. Always check if hitting a blot beats safe play before defaulting to safety. - Advance my farthest checkers (24/22, 24/20) more consistently; I keep leaving them behind when I should be bringing them in. - Don't hit blots when advancing or building a position is the stronger play. - In the home board, make room by advancing mid-point checkers rather than stacking low points. - After bringing a checker in from the bar, advance your most advanced remaining checker.

blocks.p: Game 3: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When you have a checker on the 21-point, prioritize using it to hit or build a prime rather than ignoring it and playing safe inner-board moves. - When multiple hits are available, choose the one that creates the strongest follow-up threats; hitting with a distant checker often dominates hitting with a nearby one. - Don't default to safety when a hit clearly gives you a big attacking advantage—calculate the risk properly instead of reflexively avoiding it. - After making a hit, use remaining dice to bring down higher checkers to support the attack rather than stacking points in your inner board. - The reverse also applies: sometimes a hit is "needless risk" because it doesn't generate enough follow-up; weigh both directions of the risk call.

blocks.p: Game 4: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - In races, always prioritize bringing up back checkers and advancing front checkers over moving mid-board checkers. - In endgame races, check for hitting opportunities before defaulting to safe moves. - When choosing which checker to advance, pick the one making the most net progress toward the goal. - Don't take unnecessary hits in the mid-game when advancing your prime is stronger. - When entering from the bar in a race, advance the entered checker rather than moving a mid-board one.

blocks.p: Game 5: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - With doubles, advance checkers closest to home and push through rather than stacking on intermediate points. - When choosing which checker to advance, prefer the one already closer to home over bringing a distant checker forward. - Don't force every hit — weigh the gain against the resulting vulnerability in your own position. - I'm under-advancing: "missed risk" on 4 of 7 errors. Be bolder pushing checkers into the home board. - After re-entering from the bar, consolidate rather than immediately hitting with the freed checker.

blocks.p: Game 6: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Stop hitting blots needlessly; when a safe move is available and the hit doesn't create a decisive advantage, take the safe play. - When building your home board, prioritize making new points (especially the 3-point) over adding checkers to already-occupied points. - In the mid-game transition, focus on forming a contiguous prime by moving multiple checkers into adjacent points rather than splitting across gaps.

blocks.p: Game 7: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - You miss hits far too often; when a hit is available and it's a risk situation, take it. - Don't over-commit to inner board work while back checkers remain behind; bringing them home often has higher equity. - When you re-enter from the bar, look for the hit rather than defaulting to safe play. - On doubles, remember to move back checkers even when you can advance inner ones.

blocks.p: Game 8: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When a back checker is your furthest, advance it before moving front checkers or making home points. - Take hits when available; don't default to safe moves when your board supports aggression. - In the endgame, bear off the largest checker available rather than making home points or small advances. - Once you have checkers off, focus on bearing off the remaining ones quickly instead of improving your board. - Don't expose a closed board needlessly in the endgame just to bear off a small checker.

blocks.p: Game 9: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When you have exposed back checkers, advance them before improving your inner game. - On doubles, move your most vulnerable checkers forward first; don't cluster mid-board while leaving advanced checkers exposed. - Before hitting a blot, verify the hit doesn't create a new weakness; safety often wins when the hit isn't decisive. - In the bear-off, bring in the most distant checkers first and avoid leaving unnecessary blots. - When choosing between a hit and a safe move, default to safety unless the hit clearly improves your structure.

blocks.p: Game 10: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Stop being too cautious: "missed risk" was your most frequent error type. When hitting is available and the odds favor you, take the hit. - Don't double-hit. One hit plus a safe advance usually beats two hits; evaluate if the extra hit is worth the extra exposure. - On 6-6, build points and advance inner checkers first; don't waste moves on back checkers. - When a safe play exists, use it to advance your back checkers rather than shuffling in your home board. - When choosing between hit points, prefer the one that leaves the blot harder to escape and builds your structure.

blocks.h: Series 3: 10 games, 6 won; 10 lesson calls, 0 cut, 0 empty; 0 restarts; game decisions 237, invalid 0

blocks.p: Game 1: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - You repeatedly "missed risk": when a hit or strong point-building move is available, take it instead of safe advancement. - In the endgame, bear off rather than making unnecessary points; check bearing-off options before building. - After re-entering from the bar, use the second roll to advance the re-entered checker as far as possible. - Don't move distant checkers when closer ones can consolidate in the midgame. - When advancing multiple checkers, push them through rather than stopping to make a point prematurely.

blocks.p: Game 2: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When building your home board, prioritize making and keeping higher points over advancing checkers or breaking made points to make lower ones. - In the bearing off phase, never leave a checker on an exposed high point when you can keep it on a safer lower point. - Always look for hits before bearing off, even when the safe play seems obvious.

blocks.p: Game 3: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don't hit blots unless your inner game can absorb the return; a premature hit that leaves you exposed is usually worse than a quiet advance. - When outer checkers are far behind, bring them in first rather than playing in your home board. - In the mid-game, prioritize making points and building inner structure over simply advancing a single outer checker. - When tempted to hit, ask: can I cover the return hit, and does the position still work if I'm hit? If not, play safe. - Avoid tunnel vision on one move; step back and identify the priority of the whole position before choosing.

blocks.p: Game 4: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don't make small home-board improvements while a back checker sits on 23 or 24; the engine repeatedly preferred advancing your back checkers, and your "missed risk" calls all came from this habit. - When you have a checker on the 23 point, ask: is my current move really better than bringing that checker home? If the answer isn't obvious, default to the 23 move. - Avoid over-concentrating on building the inner board (e.g., stacking 1–6 points) at the expense of bringing checkers through the prime; a strong prime plus advanced back checkers outperforms a full inner board with a stuck back checker. - On entry turns, consider moving the entry checker toward home (e.g., 22/18) rather than just hitting a distant blot; the hit is often a secondary gain.

blocks.p: Game 5: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Stop hitting reflexively; only hit when it creates a clear structural advantage (prime, blitz). Most of your large errors were needless hits that left back checkers stranded. - When you still have checkers deep in the opponent's home board, prioritize bringing them in over making contact in your own board. - In the bear-off, always advance your highest checkers first; working on lower ones while higher ones remain is a major equity leak. - After entering from the bar, use your second roll to advance that checker or develop other checkers rather than hitting from a distant point. - With doubles, prefer moving checkers through your position rather than stacking a prime that may become a liability.

blocks.p: Game 6: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When a hit is available, default to checking it seriously before choosing a quiet move. I missed or avoided hits repeatedly (Turns 7, 21, 41) when the engine wanted to strike. - Advancing checkers passively when a hit is on the table is costly; hitting often gains a prime or creates an extra shot that quiet moves sacrifice. - In the endgame, don't advance checkers into a vulnerable point just to roll them off; keep them safe to avoid being gammoned or losing a race point. - Before any midgame move, explicitly ask: "Can I hit, and does that improve my position more than the alternative?" This single question would have flagged several of my worst errors. - Distinguish "needless risk" (you should hit but chose safety) from "missed risk" (you should hit but chose a quiet advance) — both come from underweighting the value of a hit.

blocks.p: Game 7: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When bearing off, don't bear off too eagerly. Keep checkers on the 5- or 6-point when doing so is safer; premature bearing off cost you the most equity in this game. - Never ignore a distant checker. If you can advance it, do so even if it disrupts your home board structure temporarily. - Always look for the second hit before settling for one. If both rolls can hit, take both. - Preserve your prime. Don't break a point unnecessarily when you can maintain the structure with the same rolls.

blocks.p: Game 8: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When ahead, advance your mid-point checkers with 5–6 point moves rather than making small 2–3 point moves or unnecessary hits; this was my most frequent error pattern. - Hit only when it serves a concrete tactical purpose (a blot to return to, a blocked escape, or a strong follow-up); otherwise it is a needless risk. - When behind against a strong prime, accept the risk the position demands — my "missed risk" errors show I default to safety even when an aggressive move is correct.

blocks.p: Game 9: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When you have a strong home board prime, always check for hits first. I missed too many hits at the 2- and 3-point that my prime should have supported. - Advancing middle checkers into new blots is worse than hitting from a strong position; use your prime as a weapon, not just a shield. - A hit from a strong holding position is rarely "too risky" — when in doubt, hit. - When the opponent is close to bearing off, don't over-advance; keep checkers in safe positions. - When re-entering from the bar, choose the move with the best follow-up potential, not just the most advanced one.

blocks.p: Game 10: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When a hit is available, evaluate it first. I ignored three hits (turns 14, 16, 18) for a combined 0.62 equity loss. Don't default to inner board moves when a hit is on the table. - In the mid-game, hitting a lone advanced opponent checker is often worth more than consolidating your own position. - With doubles, when choosing between moving two different checkers down, prefer the higher point for more flexibility. - In the bear-off, pick the move that keeps your best rolling sequence, not just the most natural one.

blocks.p: Game 1: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - After hitting, prefer follow-up moves that keep checkers on safe points rather than creating new blots. - After entering from the bar, use your second die to advance or strengthen other checkers rather than immediately moving the re-entered one. - In the mid-game, prefer advancing checkers from higher points over creating blots in your prime or home board. - Look for hit opportunities on opponent blots before defaulting to quiet moves. - When multiple hits are available, choose the one that gives you the stronger follow-up position.

blocks.p: Game 2: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When you can make an inner point with your dice, prioritize it over advancing back checkers or taking extra hits. - When advancing checkers, push them as far as your dice allow rather than stopping at intermediate points. - Prefer advancing your most advanced checker further over making a small step on a closer one. - Avoid moving the same checker twice when spreading checkers out creates a stronger position.

blocks.p: Game 3: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When you have a checker on your 24-point (or can reach a hitting slot), always check for the hit first before moving your own checkers forward. You missed available hits three times in this game. - When bearing off on doubles, prioritize making your inner points (especially the 2-point) over bearing off extra checkers that may be hit and sent back. - In the middle game, "missed risk" errors cost far more than small positional mistakes; when the engine flags a hit, seriously consider it even if your instinct is to develop your position.

blocks.p: Game 4: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When a lone checker sits on a far outer point (23), push it forward aggressively with both dice rather than making safe inner-board moves; I "missed risk" six times this game by defaulting to safety. - In race/endgame positions, use both numbers to advance your outermost checkers as far as possible; don't waste moves rearranging inner-board points while the race is on. - Be consistent with risk: I was too aggressive once but too passive six times—when the opponent is already bearing off, the right default is usually to advance, not to stay safe. - Don't hit a blotted inner-board checker when a safe build is available with the same dice; unnecessary hits in the midgame cost real equity.

blocks.p: Game 5: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - You keep missing hitting moves by defaulting to safe plays. When a blott is available, weigh the hit seriously before falling back on passive moves. - In the middle game you leave checkers scattered and slow to build. Prioritize advancing checkers into your home board to create a prime or at least consolidate. - With quadruples, don't over-stack on a single point. Splitting down (e.g., making two separate points) gives flexibility and often primes better. - When you're behind or roughly equal, "missed risk" calls cost you. Ask: is there a checker I can push forward or a blot I can hit that GNUbg sees but I skip? - In the late game, avoid making redundant touches on the same point when you could advance a checker toward bearing off.

blocks.p: Game 6: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When a hit is available, evaluate it before defaulting to safe moves; you missed several in this game (turns 11, 17). - Don't be too passive with a lone back checker—advancing it off the 24-point is often stronger than consolidating in your own board. - After making a hit, use the second roll to advance a strong checker rather than making a weak or temporary point. - Avoid over-splitting: moving a checker two steps deep into a prime when one step would do creates needless exposure.

blocks.p: Game 7: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - After hitting, often continue advancing the hit checker rather than making a separate direct move; the advanced checker creates more threats. - I tend to be too passive in the middle game; look for aggressive options before defaulting to safe moves. - When re-entering from the bar, prefer bringing a checker home to build over making a direct shot from a remote point. - In the bear-off, avoid needless risks; the safe move is often correct even when a hit is possible. - With doubles, prefer building stacks in the home board over splitting into weaker positions.

blocks.p: Game 8: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When priming, advance checkers and strengthen the wall rather than hitting or playing in your home board. - Avoid needless hits; if a quiet advance serves your position, prefer it over creating complications. - In a winning priming game, resist playing passively in your home board—keep pushing checkers forward. - In the endgame, bring in distant checkers before over-building your home board. - When in doubt between a safe and aggressive line in a winning position, the aggressive one is often correct.

blocks.p: Game 9: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When doubles allow a double hit on a high point, take it rather than advancing back checkers that leave you with blots. - Don't hit just because you can; if a safe advance is available and the hit creates a new blot, play it safe. - In the bear-off, always move from your highest occupied point first — don't advance a lower checker when you can bear off a higher one. - When building your front, prefer advancing your most advanced checkers over stacking on lower points.

blocks.p: Game 10: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Default to advancing your most advanced checker rather than making interior moves (splits, building points). This was the dominant error pattern all game. - With doubles, use all four moves to push your most advanced checkers forward; don't waste moves on interior building. - In the endgame, bear off whenever possible instead of making holding or safety moves. - When you can advance a checker toward or past your inner board, do so before making moves that keep checkers inside.

blocks.h: Series 5: 10 games, 5 won; 10 lesson calls, 0 cut, 0 empty; 0 restarts; game decisions 240, invalid 0

blocks.p: Game 1: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don't rush checkers home; prioritize using your outer checkers to advance further before bringing others in. - Scan for hits before committing to safe advances—several missed hits cost you significant equity. - In the bearing-off, prefer the most aggressive legal play (e.g., move the innermost checker as far as possible).

blocks.p: Game 2: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Prioritize advancing your farthest checkers over small moves with inner ones; this was your most frequent error across the entire game. - Don't hit just because a hit is available; compare it against safe building moves that improve your position without added risk. - After making a hit, use your second move to advance outer checkers rather than making a small follow-up move. - When advancing in the mid-game, avoid over-extending and creating unnecessary blots on inner points.

blocks.p: Game 3: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When a hit is available, don't default to safe play—evaluate whether the hit is worth taking. blocks.pre: - Don't ignore early blots in your home board; hitting loose or advancing safely often beats passive development. - Avoid unnecessary hitting when it leaves your position stripped or inflexible; build points and keep outfield coverage. - With an opponent on the bar, balance home-board improvement against escaping back checkers before they become trapped. - When behind in the race, prioritize running both back checkers toward safety instead of making small inner-board gains. - After hitting, use the other die to improve structure or escape, not merely to stack checkers deeper.

blocks.p: Game 2: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When opponent has multiple checkers on the bar, prioritize maximum containment and board strength over hitting additional blots or advancing back checkers. - Avoid leaving unnecessary blots in your home board when you already have a commanding position; safety often outweighs marginal gains. - In bearoff preparation, maintain flexible checker distribution rather than stripping points prematurely, even when bearing off seems available. - With a racing lead and opponent's checkers trapped, focus on clean structure and avoiding shots rather than aggressive plays. - Double-check home board point-making priorities: building inner points in order (4,5,6) typically trumps making outer points or slotting.

blocks.p: Game 3: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When behind in the race, prioritize bringing back checkers home over building your inner board. - Don't hit loose in your home board when it leaves you vulnerable; sometimes quiet development is better. - With dice like 4-4 or 5-5, use all four moves to escape back checkers rather than making small home improvements. - Once your opponent is bearing off, urgency matters more than perfect board structure—run your back men immediately. - Avoid stacking checkers on the same point when you could spread them out to maintain flexibility and racing chances.

blocks.p: Game 4: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don't rush to hit loose blots in the opponent's board early; making inner-board points often beats a speculative hit that leaves your back checker split and your position undeveloped. - With an opponent on the bar, use doubles to build your board and improve structure rather than running a back checker or stripping points. - Small home-board building choices matter: prefer flexible plays that make points and keep builders over stacking checkers on an already-made point. - In the bearoff, taking a checker off is not automatic; when the opponent still has checkers back, prioritize smooth distribution and avoiding gaps to reduce later wastage and awkward rolls. - Before bearing off from a low point while your 6-point is stacked, compare simply bringing checkers down; repeated premature bearoffs cost equity even in a winning game.

blocks.p: Game 5: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don’t hit twice automatically: when the first hit already improves your position, compare a quiet second move that builds or escapes instead of leaving extra blots. - With a strong home board, use doubles to keep attacking: advancing the same rear checkers and hitting loose outfield men can outweigh tidying your inner board. - Give priority to escaping back checkers before they become trapped, especially when the opponent’s outfield blots offer a safe landing or hitting chance. - Avoid unnecessary inner-board stacking or slotting while the opponent still has timing and return shots; smooth distribution and outfield safety matter more. - Before bearing in aggressively, check the opponent’s remaining checkers and shot potential; clearing or maintaining flexibility can be better than filling deep points.

blocks.p: Game 6: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - After hitting, use the other die to improve your position—often escape a back checker—rather than automatically stacking another checker on the hit point. - When well behind in the race, split or advance back checkers to create contact; do not focus only on home-board tidying. - During a backgame, keep both anchors and coordinate their escape instead of overextending one group of runners. - Before bearing off or racing home, check whether your opponent still has checkers to escape and preserve blocking or hitting chances. - In seemingly routine late positions, verify the game score and gammon/backgammon consequences; a quiet-looking move can still be catastrophic.

blocks.p: Game 7: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Prioritize escaping back checkers over building inner-board points when behind in the race. - Look for hitting opportunities that gain tempo, especially when they also advance your back checkers. - Avoid leaving blots in your home board when safer alternatives exist. - Use doubles to mobilize back checkers instead of making small positional improvements. - When opponent has checkers on the bar, use the tempo to improve your position rather than taking unnecessary risks.

blocks.p: Game 8: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - In the opening, split your back checkers and hit loose blots in their outfield instead of quietly building your home board. - When behind or containing a back checker, run a back checker with the spare die; do not spend both dice on home-board tidying. - Before hitting deep in your board, compare it with hitting their outfield blot or escaping; deep hits can strip builders and leave you trapped. - With doubles, use all four pips to mobilize the rear checkers and make a useful outfield point, not to stack the ace-point or overstack one point. - Once the opponent is bearing off, race urgently: bring the rear checkers home with big dice instead of moving already-safe front checkers.

blocks.p: Game 9: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When behind in the race, split your back checkers early to build an anchor or escape; quiet slotting just falls further behind. - Don't bury checkers deep in your home board while your back men are stranded; keep developing the outfield and midpoint instead. - With 5-5, prioritize escaping your rear checkers over small home-board improvements; mobility beats tidiness. - Hitting loose isn't automatically right: if it leaves your back checkers trapped and strips your outfield, run instead. - After hitting from the bar, use the other die to hit again or make a point when available, not a passive shuffle.

blocks.p: Game 10: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - When opponent has blots, prioritize hitting them, especially with doubles or multiple hitting options—don't settle for safe building. - Keep your back checkers connected and avoid splitting them prematurely; advancing both together maintains flexibility and reduces risk. - Don't over-stack your home board points early; use spare checkers to build a balanced position and maintain outfield control. - With a racing lead, focus on bringing checkers home efficiently rather than making low-value home board points. - In the bearoff, prioritize taking checkers off when possible rather than rearranging your home board unnecessarily.

blocks.p: Game 4: lessons written after this game:

blocks.pre: - Don't pile extra checkers onto the 6-point or other points you already hold; use spares to slot or make new home-board points, even at some risk. - When the opponent's home board is weak or crunched, hit loose in your own board: tempo and gammon chances outweigh the cheap cost of being hit back. - Avoid leaving outfield blots when a quiet play inside your existing structure gains just as much; take risks only for a real positional gain. - Keep the midpoint while it is still useful; bring a lone outfield straggler to safety with the whole roll rather than stripping the midpoint to make a minor outfield point. - Before settling on the "safe" play, check whether the opponent can actually punish the bold one; with their checkers buried deep, play aggressively.

blocks.p: Game 5: lessons written after this game:

blocks.h: System

blocks.pre: You are a backgammon player reviewing one of your own games against the GNU Backgammon engine's evaluation, to play better in your next games. You write short, general lessons for yourself.

blocks.h: User

blocks.pre: You just played game {game} of a series of games against the same opponent. Below is the record of that game: every decision you made, with the GNU Backgammon engine's evaluation of it (2-ply: its best play, the equity you lost, and its verdict). Boards are given in your point numbering. {record} Write at most 5 lessons for your next games in this series, at most 150 words in total. Each lesson is one line starting with "- ", general advice rather than a comment on one specific position. Reply with the lessons only.
